item.title: “Good sirs, what is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair are suffering, not…
item.description:
“Good sirs, what is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair are suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering; in short, the five clinging-aggregates are suffering. This, good sirs, is called suffering. Good sirs, what is the origin of suffering? It is craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. This, good sirs, is called the origin of suffering.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 9 – Sammādiṭṭhisutta

item.title: “Once, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, monks, the quail, while being carried off by the hawk, lamented: ‘This is…
item.description:
“Once, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, monks, the quail, while being carried off by the hawk, lamented: ‘This is my misfortune! This is my lack of merit! For I wandered outside my own proper range, into the domain of others. If I had kept to my own proper range, my ancestral territory, this hawk would not have been a match for me in battle.’ - ‘What, quail, is your own proper range, your ancestral territory?’ - ‘A field plowed with a plow.’ Then, monks, the hawk, not boasting of its own strength, not pressing its own strength, released the quail and said: ‘Go, quail. Even after going there, I will not let you go.’ Then, monks, the quail went to a field plowed with a plow, climbed onto a large clod of earth, stood on it, and said to the hawk: ‘Come at me, hawk! Come at me, hawk!’ Then the hawk, boasting of its own strength, pressing its own strength, folding both wings, suddenly swooped down on the quail. When the quail knew: ‘This hawk is swooping down hard on me,’ it hid behind that clod of earth. Then, monks, the hawk shattered its own breast. So too, monks, for one who wanders outside his own proper range, into the domain of others. Therefore, monks, do not wander outside your own proper range, into the domain of others. For one who wanders outside his proper range, into the domain of others, Māra gains an opportunity, Māra gains an object.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.6

item.title: “Monks, if a monk lives without ardor in his practice, though he may wish: ‘May my mind be liberated from the defilements without clinging,’ yet…
item.description:
“Monks, if a monk lives without ardor in his practice, though he may wish: ‘May my mind be liberated from the defilements without clinging,’ yet his mind is not liberated from the defilements without clinging. Why is that? It is because he has not developed. Not developed what? He has not developed the four foundations of mindfulness. He has not developed the four right efforts. He has not developed the four bases of spiritual power. He has not developed the five faculties. He has not developed the five powers. He has not developed the seven factors of enlightenment. He has not developed the Noble Eightfold Path.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.101

item.title: “He understands thus: ‘Previously I had greed — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome. Previously I had hatred — that…
item.description:
“He understands thus: ‘Previously I had greed — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome. Previously I had hatred — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome. Previously I had delusion — that was unwholesome. Now I have none. Thus it is wholesome.’ Thus, in this very life, he is freed from longing, calm, cooled, experiencing ease, abiding in the Brahma-state himself.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.66
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Like a pit of filth Accumulated for many years — So too, a defiled person Is very hard to cleanse. Monks, know such a person…
item.description:
“Like a pit of filth
Accumulated for many years —
So too, a defiled person
Is very hard to cleanse.

Monks, know such a person —
Attached to households,
With evil desires, evil intentions,
Evil conduct, evil practices.

All of you, being of one mind,
Should shun such a person.
Blow him away like dust,
Throw him out like rubbish.

Expel the verbose one,
The fake ascetic.
Having expelled evil desires,
Evil conduct, evil practices —

Keep yourselves pure,
Live with the pure,
Mindful, dwelling together,
Wise, and make an end of suffering.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 2.6
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “If there were no gratification in form, monks, beings would not become lustful for form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become lustful…
item.description:
“If there were no gratification in form, monks, beings would not become lustful for form. But because there is gratification in form, beings become lustful for form. If there were no peril in form, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because there is peril in form, beings become disenchanted with form. If there were no escape from form, beings would not escape from form. But because there is escape from form, beings escape from form. Monks, as long as beings do not directly know as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the peril as peril, the escape as escape in regard to these six internal sense bases, they have not, monks, along with this world of devas, Māras, Brahmās, with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, dwelt with minds free from clinging, detached, liberated, unbounded. But because beings have directly known them as they actually are, therefore they have dwelt with minds free from clinging, detached, liberated, unbounded.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.18
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, what is a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future? Here, monks, a person by…
item.description:
“Monks, what is a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future? Here, monks, a person by nature has strong lust, and he constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of lust. By nature he has strong ill-will, and constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of ill-will. By nature he has strong delusion, and constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of delusion. With pain and grief, with tearful face and crying, he lives the holy life that is fully complete and pure. At the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in this realm. This, monks, is called a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 45 – Cūḷadhammasamādānasutta

item.title: “Rāhula, develop the meditation on foulness. Rāhula, by developing the meditation on foulness, what is called lust is abandoned. Rāhula, develop the meditation on impermanence.…
item.description:
“Rāhula, develop the meditation on foulness. Rāhula, by developing the meditation on foulness, what is called lust is abandoned. Rāhula, develop the meditation on impermanence. Rāhula, by developing the meditation on impermanence, what is called the conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 62 – Mahārāhulovādasutta

item.title: Elder Nun Sundarī Nandā: Nandā, look at this body — Diseased, impure, stinking. Develop the mind on foulness, One-pointed, well-concentrated. As this body, so that…
item.description:
Elder Nun Sundarī Nandā:

Nandā, look at this body —
Diseased, impure, stinking.
Develop the mind on foulness,
One-pointed, well-concentrated.

As this body, so that body —
As that body, so this body —
Foul, rotting —
Only fools delight in it.

Thus contemplate this body,
Day and night without fatigue.
With your own wisdom,
Therefore escape.
With your own wisdom,
Escape pride in beauty,
And see truly
What fools see.

This city is built of bones,
Plastered with flesh and blood.
Within dwell aging and death,
Conceit and hypocrisy.

Without heedlessness,
Rightly contemplate that body —
The true nature of this body
Is seen inside and out.
I am disenchanted with the body,
My mind is dispassionate.
Without heedlessness, free from bonds,
I am at peace, stilled.

From: Therīgāthā 5.4
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises…
item.description:
“Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises them, and dwells with lust for them, then because he delights, praises, and dwells with lust, delight arises. With the arising of delight, lust arises. With the arising of lust, bondage arises. Bound by the bondage of delight, Migajāla, that monk is called ‘one who dwells with a companion.’ Even if he lives in remote lodgings, in forests, in groves, in quiet places, with little sound, little noise, free from people’s breath, secluded, suitable for seclusion — still he is called ‘one who dwells with a companion.’ Why? Because craving, the companion, has not been abandoned by him. Therefore he is called ‘one who dwells with a companion.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.63
